entries.565e34b2fd2cf5bd0fdcbfe4149820d7ac22d90c: <div sID="gen8179" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="16" osisID="2Chr.16" sID="2Chr.16"/> <div eID="gen8179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8180" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8181" type="x-p"/> This chapter concludes the history of the reign of Asa, but does not furnish so pleasing an account of his latter end as we had of his beginning. I. Here is a foolish treaty with Benhadad king of Syria, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.1-2Chr.16.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. The reproof which God sent him for it by a prophet, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.7-2Chr.16.9">ver. 7-9</reference>. III. Asa's displeasure against the prophet for his faithfulness, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.10">ver. 10</reference>. IV. The sickness, death, and burial of Asa, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.11-2Chr.16.14">ver. 11-14</reference>.
entries.4aad851751bece8e4472599ceea5b2c6dc8e5068: <div eID="gen8181" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8180" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Asa's League with Benhadad. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 929.)</title> <div sID="gen8182" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> In the six and thirtieth year of the reign of Asa Baasha king of Israel came up against Judah, and built Ramah, to the intent that he might let none go out or come in to Asa king of Judah. <hi type="super">2</hi> Then Asa brought out silver and gold out of the treasures of the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> and of the king's house, and sent to Ben-hadad king of Syria, that dwelt at Damascus, saying, <hi type="super">3</hi> <hi type="italic">There is</hi> a league between me and thee, as <hi type="italic">there was</hi> between my father and thy father: behold, I have sent thee silver and gold; go, break thy league with Baasha king of Israel, that he may depart from me. <hi type="super">4</hi> And Ben-hadad hearkened unto king Asa, and sent the captains of his armies against the cities of Israel; and they smote Ijon, and Dan, and Abel-maim, and all the store cities of Naphtali. <hi type="super">5</hi> And it came to pass, when Baasha heard <hi type="italic">it,</hi> that he left off building of Ramah, and let his work cease. <hi type="super">6</hi> Then Asa the king took all Judah; and they carried away the stones of Ramah, and the timber thereof, wherewith Baasha was building; and he built therewith Geba and Mizpah. <div eID="gen8182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8183" type="x-p"/> How to reconcile the date of this event with the history of the kings I am quite at a loss. Baasha died in the twenty-sixth year of Asa, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.8">1 Kings xvi. 8</reference>. How then could this be done in his thirty-sixth year, when Baasha's family was quite cut off, and Omri was upon the throne? It is generally said to be meant of the thirty-sixth year of the kingdom of Asa, namely, that of Judah, beginning from the first of Rehoboam, and so it coincides with the sixteenth of Asa's reign; but then (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.19">ch. xv. 19</reference> must be so understood; and how could it be spoken of as a great thing that there was no more war till the fifteenth year of Asa, when that passage immediately before was in his fifteenth year? (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.10">ch. xv. 10</reference>), and after this miscarriage of his, here recorded, he had wars, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.9">v. 9</reference>. Josephus places it in his twenty-sixth year, and then we must suppose a mistake in the transcriber here and (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.19">ch. xv. 19</reference>, the admission of which renders the computation easy. This passage we had before (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.17-1Kgs.15.24">1 Kings xv. 17</reference>, &c.) and Asa was in several ways faulty in it. 1. He did not do well to make a league with Benhadad, a heathen king, and to value himself so much upon it as he seems to have done, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.3">v. 3</reference>. Had he relied more upon his covenant, and his father's, with God, he would not have boasted so much of his league, and his father's, with the royal family of Syria. 2. If he had had a due regard to the honour of Israel in general, he would have found some other expedient to give Baasha a diversion than by calling in a foreign force, and inviting into the country a common enemy, who, in process of time, might be a plague to Judah too. 3. It was doubtless a sin in Benhadad to break his league with Baasha upon no provocation, but merely through the influence of a bribe; and, if so, certainly it was a sin in Asa to move him to it, especially to hire him to do it. The public faith of kings and kingdoms must not be made so cheap a thing. 4. To take silver and gold out of the house of the Lord for this purpose was a great aggravation of the sin, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.2">v. 2</reference>. Must the temple be plundered to serve his carnal politics? He had better have brought gifts and offerings with prayers and supplications, to the house of the Lord, that he might have engaged God on his side and made him his friend; then he would not have needed to be at this expense to make Benhadad his friend. 5. It was well if Asa had not to answer for all the mischief that the army of Benhadad did unjustly to the cities of Israel, all the blood they shed and all the spoil they made, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.4">v. 4</reference>. Perhaps Asa intended not that they should carry the matter so far. But those that draw others to sin know not what they do, nor where it will end. The beginning of sin is as the letting forth of water. However the project succeeded. Benhadad gave Baasha a powerful diversion, obliged him to leave off building Ramah and betake himself to the defence of his own country northward, which gave Asa an opportunity, not only to demolish his fortifications, but to seize the materials and convert them to his own use.
entries.3dd98fe2548532dcf81ce5e197143793addbcf08: <div eID="gen8183" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Asa's Death and Burial. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 914.)</title> <div sID="gen8184" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> And at that time Hanani the seer came to Asa king of Judah, and said unto him, Because thou hast relied on the king of Syria, and not relied on the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God, therefore is the host of the king of Syria escaped out of thine hand. <hi type="super">8</hi> Were not the Ethiopians and the Lubims a huge host, with very many chariots and horsemen? yet, because thou didst rely on the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , he delivered them into thine hand. <hi type="super">9</hi> For the eyes of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to show himself strong in the behalf of <hi type="italic">them</hi> whose heart <hi type="italic">is</hi> perfect toward him. Herein thou hast done foolishly: therefore from henceforth thou shalt have wars. <hi type="super">10</hi> Then Asa was wroth with the seer, and put him in a prison house; for <hi type="italic">he was</hi> in a rage with him because of this <hi type="italic">thing.</hi> And Asa oppressed <hi type="italic">some</hi> of the people the same time. <hi type="super">11</hi> And, behold, the acts of Asa, first and last, lo, they <hi type="italic">are</hi> written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel. <hi type="super">12</hi> And Asa in the thirty and ninth year of his reign was diseased in his feet, until his disease <hi type="italic">was</hi> exceeding <hi type="italic">great:</hi> yet in his disease he sought not to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , but to the physicians. <hi type="super">13</hi> And Asa slept with his fathers, and died in the one and fortieth year of his reign. <hi type="super">14</hi> And they buried him in his own sepulchres, which he had made for himself in the city of David, and laid him in the bed which was filled with sweet odours and divers kinds <hi type="italic">of spices</hi> prepared by the apothecaries' art: and they made a very great burning for him. <div eID="gen8184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8185" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A plain and faithful reproof given to Asa by a prophet of the Lord, for making this league with Baasha. The reprover was Hanani the seer, the father of Jehu, another prophet, whom we read of <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.2">2 Chron. xix. 2</reference>. We observed several things amiss in Asa's treaty with Benhadad. But that which the prophet here charges upon him as the greatest fault he was guilty of in that matter is his <hi type="italic">relying on the king of Syria and not on the Lord his God, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.7">v. 7</reference>.</hi> He thought that, though God was on his side, this would not stand him in stead unless he had Benhadad on his side, that God either could not or would not help him, but he must take this indirect course to help himself. Note, God is much displeased when he is distrusted and when an arm of flesh is relied on more than his power and goodness. By putting our confidence in God we give honour to him, and therefore he thinks himself affronted if we give that honour to another. He plainly tells the king that herein he had done foolishly, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.9">v. 9</reference>. It is a foolish thing to lean on a broken reed, when we have the rock of ages to rely upon. To convince him of his folly he shows him, <div eID="gen8185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8186" type="x-p"/> 1. That he acted against his experience, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.8">v. 8</reference>. He, of all men, had no reason to distrust God, who had found him such a present powerful helper, by whom he had been made to triumph over a threatening enemy, as his father before him, <hi type="italic">because he relied upon the Lord his God,</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.18">ch. xiii. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.11">xiv. 11</reference>. "<hi type="italic">What!</hi>" said the prophet, "Were not the Ethiopians and the Lubim a huge host, enough to swallow up a kingdom? And yet, <hi type="italic">because thou didst rely on the Lord, he delivered them into thy hand;</hi> and was not he sufficient to help thee against Baasha?" Note, The many experiences we have had of the goodness of God to us aggravate our distrust of him. Has he not helped us in six troubles? And have we any reason to suspect him in the seventh? But see how deceitful our hearts are! We trust in God when we have nothing else to trust to, when need drives us to him; but, when we have other things to stay on, we are apt to stay too much on them and to lean on our own understanding as long as that has any thing to offer; but a believing confidence will be in God only, when a smiling world courts it most. <div eID="gen8186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8187" type="x-p"/> 2. That he acted against his knowledge of God and his providence, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.9">v. 9</reference>. Asa could not be ignorant that <hi type="italic">the eyes of the Lord run to and fro through the earth, strongly to hold with those</hi> (so it may be read) <hi type="italic">whose heart is perfect towards him;</hi> that is, (1.) That God governs the world in infinite wisdom, and the creatures, and all their actions, are continually under his eye. The eye of Providence is quick-sighted—it <hi type="italic">runs;</hi> it is intent—it runs <hi type="italic">to and fro;</hi> it reaches far—<hi type="italic">through the whole earth,</hi> no corner of which is from under it, not the most dark or distant; and his eye directs his hand, and the arm of his power; for he shows himself strong. Does Satan walk to and fro in the earth? Providence <hi type="italic">runs</hi> to and fro, is never out of the way, never to seek, never at a loss. (2.) That God governs the world for the good of his people, does all in pursuance of the counsels of his love concerning their salvation, all <hi type="italic">for Jacob his servant's sake, and Israel his elect,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.45.4">Isa. xlv. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">Christ is head over all things to his church,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.22">Eph. i. 22</reference>. (3.) That those whose hearts are upright with him may be sure of his protection and have all the reason in the world to depend upon it. He is able to protect them in the way of their duty (for wisdom and might are his), and he actually intends their protection. A practical disbelief of this is at the bottom of all our departures from God and double-dealing with him. Asa could not trust God and therefore made court to Benhadad. <div eID="gen8187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8188" type="x-p"/> 3. That he acted against his interest. (1.) He had lost an opportunity of checking the growing greatness of the king of Syria, (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.7">v. 7</reference>): His <hi type="italic">host has escaped out of thy hand,</hi> which otherwise would have joined with Baasha's and fallen with it. (2.) He had incurred God's displeasure and henceforth must expect no peace, but the constant alarms of war, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.9">v. 9</reference>. Those that cannot find in their hearts to trust God forfeit his protection and throw themselves out of it. <div eID="gen8188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8189" type="x-p"/> II. Asa's displeasure at this reproof. Though it came from God by one that was known to be his messenger, though the reproof was just and the reasoning fair, and all intended for his good, yet he was wroth with the seer for telling him of his folly; nay, <hi type="italic">he was in a rage with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.10">v. 10</reference>. Is this Asa? Is this he whose heart was perfect with the Lord all his days? Well, let him that thinks he stands take heed lest he fall. A wise man, and yet in a rage! An Israelite, and yet in a rage with a prophet! A good man, and yet impatient of reproof, and that cannot bear to be told of his faults! Lord, what is man, when God leaves him to himself? Those that idolize their own conduct cannot bear contradiction; and those that indulge a peevish passionate temper may be transported by it into impieties as well as into indecencies, and will, some time or other, fly in the face of God himself. See what gall and wormwood this root of bitterness bore. 1. In his rage he committed the prophet to the jail, <hi type="italic">put him in a prison-house,</hi> as a malefactor, <hi type="italic">in the stocks</hi> (so some read it,) or into <hi type="italic">little-ease.</hi> God's prophets meet with many that cannot bear reproof, but take it much amiss, yet they must do their duty. 2. Having proceeded thus far, <hi type="italic">he oppressed some of the people,</hi> probably such as owned the prophet in his sufferings, or were known to be his particular friends. He that abused his power for the persecuting of God's prophet was left to himself further to abuse it for the crushing of his own subjects, whereby he weakened himself and lost his interest. Most persecutors have been tyrants. <div eID="gen8189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8190" type="x-p"/> III. His sickness. Two years before he died <hi type="italic">he was diseased in his feet</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.12">v. 12</reference>), afflicted with the gout in a high degree. He had put the prophet in the stocks, and now God put him in the stocks; so his punishment answered his sin. <hi type="italic">His disease was exceedingly great;</hi> it came to the height (so some); it flew up to his head (so others), and then it was mortal. This was his affliction; but his sin was that in his disease, instead of seeking to the Lord for relief, he <hi type="italic">sought to the physicians.</hi> His making use of physicians was his duty; but trusting to them, and expecting that from them which was to be had from God only, were his sin and folly. The help of creatures must always be used with an eye to the Creator, and in dependence upon him, who makes every creature that to us which it is, and without whom the most skilful and faithful are physicians of no value. Some think that these physicians were strangers to the commonwealth of Israel, and were a sort of conjurers, to whom he applied as if there were not a God in Israel. <div eID="gen8190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8191" type="x-p"/> IV. His death and burial. His funeral had something of extraordinary solemnity in it, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.14">v. 14</reference>. They made a very magnificent <hi type="italic">burying for him.</hi> I am loth to think (as some do) that he himself ordered this funeral pomp, and that it was an instance of his vanity, that he would be buried like the Gentiles, and not after the way of the Jews. It is said indeed, <hi type="italic">He digged the sepulchre for himself,</hi> as one mindful of his grave; but I am willing to believe that this funeral pomp was rather an expression of the great respect his people retained for him, notwithstanding the failings and infirmities of his latter days. It was agreed to do him honour at his death. Note, The eminent piety and usefulness of good men ought to be remembered to their praise, though they have had their blemishes. Let their faults be buried in their graves, while their services are remembered over their graves. He that said, <hi type="italic">There is not a just man that doeth good and sinneth not, yet</hi> said also, <hi type="italic">The memory of the just is blessed;</hi> and let it be so.  <chapter eID="2Chr.16"/> <div eID="gen8191" type="x-p"/>

entries.f606ed57ecc689ab8967acab05d6f9e564aad13f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4024"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 16</title> <div sID="gen5823" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.1-2Chr.16.14">2Ch 16:1-14</reference>. Asa, by a League with the Syrians, Diverts Baasha from Building Ramah.<div eID="gen5823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5824" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4024"/><hi type="bold">1-6. In the six and thirtieth year of the reign of Asa, Baasha ... came up against Judah--</hi>Baasha had died several years before this date (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.33">1Ki 15:33</reference>), and the best biblical critics are agreed in considering this date to be calculated from the separation of the kingdoms, and coincident with the sixteenth year of Asa's reign. This mode of reckoning was, in all likelihood, generally followed in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel, the public annals of the time (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.11">2Ch 16:11</reference>), the source from which the inspired historian drew his account.<div eID="gen5824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5825" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Baasha ... built Ramah--</hi>that is, fortified it. The blessing of God which manifestly rested at this time on the kingdom of Judah, the signal victory of Asa, the freedom and purity of religious worship, and the fame of the late national covenant, were regarded with great interest throughout Israel, and attracted a constantly increasing number of emigrants to Judah. Baasha, alarmed at this movement, determined to stem the tide; and as the high road to and from Jerusalem passed by Ramah, he made that frontier town, about six miles north of Asa's capital, a military station, where the vigilance of his sentinels would effectually prevent all passage across the boundary of the kingdom (see on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.16-1Kgs.15.22">1Ki 15:16-22</reference>; also <reference osisRef="Jer.41.9">Jr 41:9</reference>). <div eID="gen5825" type="x-p"/>
entries.83499ca0ecba859674481ab28706373aabb033c1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4026"/><div sID="gen5827" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4026"/><hi type="bold">7-10. Hanani the seer came to Asa ... and said--</hi>His object was to show the king his error in forming his recent league with Ben-hadad. The prophet represented the appropriation of the temple treasures to purchase the services of the Syrian mercenaries, as indicating a distrust in God most blameable with the king's experience. He added, that in consequence of this want of faith, Asa had lost the opportunity of gaining a victory over the united forces of Baasha and Ben-hadad, more splendid than that obtained over the Ethiopians. Such a victory, by destroying their armies, would have deprived them of all power to molest him in the future; whereas by his foolish and worldly policy, so unworthy of God's vicegerent, to misapply the temple treasures and corrupt the fidelity of an ally of the king of Israel, he had tempted the cupidity of the one, and increased the hostility of the other, and rendered himself liable to renewed troubles (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.32">1Ki 15:32</reference>). This rebuke was pungent and, from its truth and justness, ought to have penetrated and afflicted the heart of such a man as Asa. But his pride was offended at the freedom taken by the honest reprover of royalty, and in a burst of passionate resentment, he ordered Hanani to be thrown into prison. <div eID="gen5827" type="x-p"/>
entries.c52dd61f8185ede92d055e0c9c35c9d2f11f4884: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4028"/><div sID="gen5829" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4028"/><hi type="bold">12. Asa ... was diseased in his feet--</hi>probably the gout.<div eID="gen5829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5830" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yet his disease was exceeding great--</hi>better, "moved upwards" in his body, which proves the violent and dangerous type of the malady.<div eID="gen5830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5831" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yet in his disease he sought not to the Lord, but to the physicians--</hi>most probably Egyptian physicians, who were anciently in high repute at foreign courts, and who pretended to expel diseases by charms, incantations, and mystic arts. Asa's fault consisted in his trusting to such physicians, while he neglected to supplicate the aid and blessing of God. The best and holiest men have been betrayed for a time into sins, but through repentance have risen again; and as Asa is pronounced a good man (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.17">2Ch 15:17</reference>), it may be presumed that he also was restored to a better state of mind. <div eID="gen5831" type="x-p"/>
entries.618c27845a9f65c4ec0be901d2ef6451ffd8ab3e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4029"/><div sID="gen5832" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4029"/><hi type="bold">14. they buried him in his own sepulchres--</hi>The tombs in the neighborhood of Jerusalem were excavated in the side of a rock. One cave contained several tombs or sepulchres.<div eID="gen5832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5833" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">laid him in the bed ... filled with sweet odours and divers kinds of spices--</hi>It is evident that a sumptuous public funeral was given him as a tribute of respect and gratitude for his pious character and patriotic government. But whether "the bed" means a state couch on which he lay exposed to public view, the odoriferous perfumes being designed to neutralize the offensive smell of the corpse, or whether it refers to an embalmment, in which aromatic spices were always used in great profusion, it is impossible to say.<div eID="gen5833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5834" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they made a very great burning for him--</hi>according to some, for consuming the spices. According to others, it was a magnificent pile for the cremation of the corpse--a usage which was at that time, and long after, prevalent among the Hebrews, and the omission of which in the case of royal personages was reckoned a great indignity (<reference osisRef="2Chr.21.19">2Ch 21:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.12">1Sa 31:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.34.5">Jr 34:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.6.10">Am 6:10</reference>). <chapter eID="2Chr.16"/>

entries.69268f439c60b037d68a8d1ec69b759292972b9e: <div eID="gen14249" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen14250" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14251" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14251" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14250" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14252" type="x-p"/> Baasha, king of Israel, begins to build Ramah, to prevent his subjects from having any intercourse with the Jews, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.1">2Chr 16:1</reference>. Asa hires Ben-hadad, king of Syria, against him; and obliges him to leave off building Ramah, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.2-2Chr.16.5">2Chr 16:2-5</reference>. Asa and his men carry the stones and timbers of Ramah away, and build therewith Geba and Mizpah, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.6">2Chr 16:6</reference>. Asa is reproved by Hanani, the seer, for his union with the king of Syria: he is offended with the seer, and puts him in prison, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.7-2Chr.16.10">2Chr 16:7-10</reference>. Of his acts, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.11">2Chr 16:11</reference>. He is diseased in his feet, and seeks to physicians and not to God, and dies, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.12">2Chr 16:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.13">2Chr 16:13</reference>. His sumptuous funeral, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.14">2Chr 16:14</reference>. <div eID="gen14252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14253" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen14253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14254" type="x-p"/> The six and thirtieth year - After the division of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah; according to Usher. This opinion is followed in our margin; see the note on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.16">1Kgs 15:16</reference>, where this subject is farther considered. <div eID="gen14254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14255" type="x-p"/> Concerning Baasha's building of Ramah, see the note on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.17">1Kgs 15:17</reference>.
entries.e89f0b8077223e29dbdb3f93b89b4eae0999f5cb: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen14255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14256" type="x-p"/> There is a league - Let there be a treaty, offensive and defensive, between me and thee: see on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.22">1Kgs 15:22</reference> (note).
entries.d2d336ef22acbaee04ad470d233cbe0dd77fc799: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen14256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14257" type="x-p"/> Took all Judah - See on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.22">1Kgs 15:22</reference> (note).
entries.40a5c685b09bca8d63d22c6d4eca28b9acc1c650: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen14257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14258" type="x-p"/> Escaped out of thine hand - It is difficult to know what is here intended. Perhaps the Divine providence had intended to give Asa a grand victory over the Syrians, who had always been the inveterate enemies of the Jews; but by this unnecessary and very improper alliance between Asa and Ben-hadad, this purpose of the Divine providence was prevented, and thus the Syrians escaped out of his hands.
entries.5af8cb5f694277d7515d7b3723104d338d07cfdf: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen14258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14259" type="x-p"/> Therefore - thou shalt have wars - And so he had with Israel during the rest of his reign, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.32">1Kgs 15:32</reference>.
entries.918148ad9e8208340f955188fae509cec0404088: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen14259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14260" type="x-p"/> Asa was wroth with the seer - Instead of humbling himself, and deprecating the displeasure of the Lord, he persecuted his messenger: and having thus laid his impious hands upon the prophet, he appears to have got his heart hardened through the deceitfulness of sin; and then he began to oppress the people, either by unjust imprisonments, or excessive taxations.
entries.4d5f269510a565da2fbba4da12bbe3c2a319c02b: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen14260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14261" type="x-p"/> Diseased in his feet - He had a strong and long fit of the gout; this is most likely. <div eID="gen14261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14262" type="x-p"/> He sought not to the Lord - "He did not seek discipline from the face of the Lord, but from the physicians." - Targum. <div eID="gen14262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14263" type="x-p"/> Are we not taught by this to make prayer and supplication to the Lord in our afflictions, with the expectation that he will heal us when he finds us duly humbled, i.e., when the end is answered for which he sends the affliction?
entries.01c3a791a07d52b93c5ff9e0335836b154f8a6cb: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen14263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14264" type="x-p"/> And laid him in the bed - It is very likely that the body of Asa was burnt; that the bed spoken of here was a funeral pyre, on which much spices and odoriferous woods had been placed; and then they set fire to the whole and consumed the body with the aromatics. Some think the body was not burned, but the aromatics only, in honor of the king. <div eID="gen14264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14265" type="x-p"/> How the ancients treated the bodies of the illustrious dead we learn from Virgil, in the funeral rites paid to Misenus. <div eID="gen14265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14266" type="x-p"/> Nec minus interea Misenum in littore Teucri <div eID="gen14266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14267" type="x-p"/> Flebant, et cineri ingrato suprema ferebant. <div eID="gen14267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14268" type="x-p"/> Principio pinguem taedis et robore secto <div eID="gen14268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14269" type="x-p"/> Ingentem struxere pyram: cui frondibus atris <div eID="gen14269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14270" type="x-p"/> Intexunt latera, et ferales ante cupressas <div eID="gen14270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14271" type="x-p"/> Constituunt, decorantque super fulgentibus armis, etc. <div eID="gen14271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14272" type="x-p"/> Aen. vi. 214. "Meanwhile the Trojan troops, with weeping eyes, <div eID="gen14272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14273" type="x-p"/> To dead Misenus pay their obsequies. <div eID="gen14273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14274" type="x-p"/> First from the ground a lofty pile they rear <div eID="gen14274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14275" type="x-p"/> Of pitch trees, oaks, and pines, and unctuous fir. <div eID="gen14275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14276" type="x-p"/> The fabric's front with cypress twigs they strew, <div eID="gen14276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14277" type="x-p"/> And stick the sides with boughs of baleful yew. <div eID="gen14277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14278" type="x-p"/> The topmost part his glittering arms adorn: <div eID="gen14278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14279" type="x-p"/> Warm waters, then, in brazen caldrons borne <div eID="gen14279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14280" type="x-p"/> Are poured to wash his body joint by joint, <div eID="gen14280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14281" type="x-p"/> And fragrant oils the stiffen'd limbs anoint. <div eID="gen14281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14282" type="x-p"/> With groans and cries Misenus they deplore: <div eID="gen14282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14283" type="x-p"/> Then on a bier, with purple cover'd o'er, <div eID="gen14283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14284" type="x-p"/> The breathless body thus bewail'd they lay, <div eID="gen14284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14285" type="x-p"/> And fire the pile (their faces turn'd away). <div eID="gen14285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14286" type="x-p"/> Such reverend rites their fathers used to pay. <div eID="gen14286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14287" type="x-p"/> Pure oil and incense on the fire they throw, <div eID="gen14287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14288" type="x-p"/> And fat of victims which their friends bestow. <div eID="gen14288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14289" type="x-p"/> These gifts the greedy flames to dust devour, <div eID="gen14289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14290" type="x-p"/> Then on the living coals red wine they pour. <div eID="gen14290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14291" type="x-p"/> And last the relics by themselves dispose, <div eID="gen14291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14292" type="x-p"/> Which in a brazen urn the priests enclose. <div eID="gen14292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14293" type="x-p"/> Old Corineus compass'd thrice the crew, <div eID="gen14293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14294" type="x-p"/> And dipp'd an olive branch in holy dew; <div eID="gen14294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14295" type="x-p"/> Which thrice he sprinkled round, and thrice aloud <div eID="gen14295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14296" type="x-p"/> Invoked the dead, and then dismiss'd the crowd." <div eID="gen14296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14297" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen14297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14298" type="x-p"/> All these rites are of Asiatic extraction. Virgil borrows almost every circumstance from Homer; (see Iliad, xxiii., ver. 164, etc.); and we well know that Homer ever describes Asiatic manners. Sometimes, especially in war, several captives were sacrificed to the manes of the departed hero. So, in the place above, the mean-souled, ferocious demon, Achilles, is represented sacrificing twelve Trojan captives to the ghost of his friend Patroclus. Urns containing the ashes and half-calcined bones of the dead occur frequently in barrows or tumuli in this country; most of them, no doubt, the work of the Romans. But all ancient nations, in funeral matters, have nearly the same rites.  <chapter eID="2Chr.16"/> <div eID="gen14298" type="x-p"/>

entries.9753c3f17502441153570fcf1c0c14db45efdc27: <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.1-2Chr.16.5">2Ch 16:1-5</reference> <hi type="italic">War with Baasha, and the weakness of Asa’s faith. The end of his reign.</hi> - <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.1">2Ch 16:1</reference>-6. Baasha’s invasion of Judah, and Asa’s prayer for help to the king of Syria. The statement, “In the thirty-sixth year of the reign of Asa, Baasha the king of Israel came up against Judah,” is inaccurate, or rather cannot possibly be correct; for, according to 1Ki 16:8, 1Ki 16:10, Baasha died in the twenty-sixth year of Asa’s reign, and his successor Elah was murdered by Zimri in the second year of his reign, i.e., in the twenty-seventh year of Asa. The older commentators, for the most part, accepted the conjecture that the thirty-fifth year (in <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.19">2Ch 15:19</reference>) is to be reckoned from the commencement of the kingdom of Judah; and consequently, since Asa became king in the twentieth year of the kingdom of Judah, that Baasha’s invasion occurred in the sixteenth year of his reign, and that the land had enjoyed peace till his fifteenth year; cf. Ramb. <hi type="italic">ad h. l.;</hi> des Vignoles, <hi type="italic">Chronol.</hi> i. p. 299. This is in substance correct; but the statement, “in the thirty-sixth year of Asa’s kingship,” cannot re reconciled with it. For even if we suppose that the author of the Chronicle derived his information from an authority which reckoned from the rise of the kingdom of Judah, yet it could not have been said on that authority, אסא למלכוּת. This only the author of the Chronicle can have written; but then he cannot also have taken over the statement, “in the thirty-sixth year,” unaltered from his authority into his book. There remains therefore no alternative but to regard the text as erroneous - the letters ל (30) and י (10), which are somewhat similar in the ancient Hebrew characters, having been interchanged by a copyist; and hence the numbers 35 and 36 have arisen out of the original 15 and 16. By this alteration all difficulties are removed, and all the statements of the Chronicle as to Asa’s reign are harmonized. During the first ten years there was peace (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.1">2Ch 14:1</reference>); thereafter, in the eleventh year, the inroad of the Cushites; and after the victory over them there was the continuation of the Cultus reform, and rest until the fifteenth year, in which the renewal of the covenant took place (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.19">2Ch 15:19</reference>, cf. with <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.10">2Ch 15:10</reference>); and in the sixteenth year the war with Baasha arose.<note placement="foot">Movers, S. 255ff., and Then. on 1 Kings 15, launch out into arbitrary hypotheses, founded in both cases upon the erroneous presumption that the author of the Chronicle copied our canonical books of Kings - they being his authority-partly misunderstanding and partly altering them.</note> <div eID="gen6027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6028" type="x-p"/> The account of this war in <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.1-2Chr.16.6">2Ch 16:1-6</reference> agrees with that in 1Ki 15:17-22 almost literally, and has been commented upon in the remarks on 1 Kings 15. In <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.2">2Ch 16:2</reference> the author of the Chronicle has mentioned only the main things. Abel-maim, i.e., Abel in the Water (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.4">2Ch 16:4</reference>), is only another name for Abel-Beth-Maachah (Kings); see on 2Sa 20:14. In the same verse נפתּלי ערי כּל־מסכּנות ואת is surprising, “and all magazines (or stores) of the cities of Naphtali,” instead of נפתּלי כּל־ארץ על כּל־כּנּרות את, “all Kinneroth, together with all the land of Naphtali” (Kings). Then. and Berth. think ערי מסכנות has arisen out of ארץ and כנרות by a misconception of the reading; while Gesen., Dietr. in <hi type="italic">Lex. sub voce</hi> כּנּרות, conjecture that in 1Ki 15:20 מסכּנות should be read instead of כּנּרות. Should the difference actually be the result only of a misconception, then the latter conjecture would have much more in its favour than the first. But it is a more probable solution of the difficulty that the text of the Chronicle is a translation of the unusual and, especially on account of the כּל־ארץ נ על, scarcely intelligible כּל־כּנּרות. כּנּרות is the designation of the very fertile district on the west side of the Sea of Kinnereth, i.e., Gennesaret, after which a city also was called כּנּרת (see on <reference osisRef="Josh.19.35">Jos 19:35</reference>), and which, on account of its fertility, might be called the granary of the tribal domain of Naphtali. But the smiting of a district can only be a devastation of it, - a plundering and destruction of its produce, both in stores and elsewhere. With this idea the author of the Chronicle, instead of the district Kinnereth, the name of which had perhaps become obsolete in his time, speaks of the מסכּנות, the magazines or stores, of the cities of Naphtali. In <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.5">2Ch 16:5</reference>, too, we cannot hold the addition את־מלאכתּו ויּשׁבּת, “he caused his work to rest,” as Berth. does, for an interpretation of the original reading, בּתרצה ויּשׁב (Kings), it having become illegible: it is rather a free rendering of the thought that Baasha abandoned his attempt upon Judah.
entries.f991da4c60ba6aa43c507f8c7000e5d58a976846: <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.6">2Ch 16:6</reference> <div eID="gen6028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6029" type="x-p"/> In regard to the building of Mizpah, it is casually remarked in <reference osisRef="Jer.41.9">Jer 41:9</reference> that Asa had there built a cistern.
entries.a5164094ce8659b7db3c2e25a8a00c4d20115501: <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.7-2Chr.16.8">2Ch 16:7-8</reference> <hi type="italic">The rebuke of the prophet Hanani, and Asa’s crime</hi>. - 2Ch 16:7. The prophet Hanani is met with only here. Jehu, the son of Hanani, who announced to Baasha the ruin of his house (1Ki 16:1), and who reappears under Jehoshaphat (<reference osisRef="2Chr.19.2">2Ch 19:2</reference>), was without doubt his son. Hanani said to King Asa, “Because thou hast relied on the king of Aram, and not upon Jahve thy God, therefore is the host of the king of Aram escaped out of thy hand.” Berth. has correctly given the meaning thus: “that Asa, if he had relied upon God, would have conquered not only the host of Baasha, but also the host of the king of Damascus, if he had, as was to be feared, in accordance with his league with Baasha (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.3">2Ch 16:3</reference>), in common with Israel, made an attack upon the kingdom of Judah.” To confirm this statement, the prophet points to the victory over the great army of the Cushites, which Asa had won by his trust in God the Lord. With the Cushites Hanani names also פּרשׁים, Libyans (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.12.3">2Ch 12:3</reference>), and besides רכב, the war-chariots, also פּרשׁים osla ,sto, horsemen, in order to portray the enemy rhetorically, while in the historical narrative only the immense number of warriors and the multitude of the chariots is spoken of.
entries.371b0dc12d9427ac57e959d082cac8555cf4e73d: <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.9">2Ch 16:9</reference> “For Jahve, His eyes run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to show Himself strong with those whose heart is devoted to Him;” i.e., for Jahve, who looks forth over all the earth, uses every opportunity wonderfully to succour those who are piously devoted to Him. עם התחזק, to help mightily, as in 1Ch 11:10. אליו שׁלם עם־לבבם is a relative sentence without the relative אשׁר with עם; cf. 1Ch 15:12. “Thou hast done foolishly, therefore,” <hi type="italic">scil.</hi> because thou hast set thy trust upon men instead of upon Jahve, “for from henceforth there shall be wars to thee” (thou shalt have war). In these words the prophet does not announce to Asa definite wars, but only expresses the general idea that Asa by his godless policy would bring only wars (מלחמות in indefinite universality), not peace, to the kingdom. History confirms the truth of this announcement, although we have no record of any other wars which broke out under Asa.
entries.1e9aefa610d0cb6bab0846c171a8658ac9e1ecf8: <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.10">2Ch 16:10</reference> <div eID="gen6029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6030" type="x-p"/> This sharp speech so angered the king, that he caused the seer to be set in the stock-house. המּהשפכת בּית, properly, house of stocks. מהפּכת, twisting, is an instrument of torture, a stock, by which the body was forced into an unnatural twisted position, the victim perhaps being bent double, with the hands and feet fastened together: cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.20.2">Jer 20:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.26">Jer 29:26</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Acts.16.24">Act 16:24</reference>, ἔβαλεν εἰς τὴν φυλακὴ̀ν καὶ τοὺς πόδας ἠσφαλίσατο αὐτῶν εἰς τὸ ξύλον. “For in wrath against him (<hi type="italic">scil.</hi> he did it) because of this thing, and Asa crushed some of the people at this time.” Clearly Hanani’s speech, and still more Asa’s harsh treatment of the seer, caused great discontent among the people, at least in the upper classes, so that the king felt himself compelled to use force against them. רצץ, to break or crush, is frequently used along with עשׁק (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.33">Deu 28:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.3">1Sa 12:3</reference>, etc.), and signifies to suppress with violence. Asa had indeed well deserved the censure, Thou hast dealt foolishly. His folly consisted in this, that in order to get help against Baasha’s attack, he had had recourse to a means which must become dangerous to him and to his kingdom; for it was not difficult to foresee that the Syrian king Benhadad would turn the superiority to Israel which he had gained against Judah itself. But in order to estimate rightly Asa’s conduct, we must consider that it was perhaps an easier thing, in human estimation, to conquer the innumerable multitudes of the Ethiopian hordes than the united forces of the kings of Israel and Syria; and that, notwithstanding the victory over the Ethiopians, yet Asa’s army may have been very considerably weakened by that war. But these circumstances are not sufficient to justify Asa. Since he had so manifestly had the help of the Lord in the war against the Cushites, it was at bottom mainly weakness of faith, or want of full trust in the omnipotence of the Lord, which caused him to seek the help of the enemy of God’s people, the king of Syria, instead of that of the Almighty God, and to make flesh his arm; and for this he was justly censured by the prophet.
entries.b31a86e4f1460885214d113688d190822ab031f3: <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.11">2Ch 16:11</reference> <hi type="italic">The end of Asa’s reign;</hi> cf. 1Ki 15:23-24. - On <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.11">2Ch 16:11</reference>, cf. the Introduction.
entries.1342844bd161d5e11e33eff9b202c00ab4c82b7f: <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.12-2Chr.16.13">2Ch 16:12-13</reference> <div eID="gen6030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6031" type="x-p"/> In the thirty-ninth year of his reign Asa became diseased in his feet, and that in a high degree. The words חיו עד־למעלה are a circumstantial clause: to a high degree was his sickness. “And also in his sickness (as in the war against Baasha) he sought not Jahve, but turned to the physicians.” דּרשׁ is primarily construed with the accus., as usually in connection with יהוה or אלהים, to seek God, to come before Him with prayer and supplication; then with בּ, as usually of an oracle, or seeking help of idols (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.7">1Sa 28:7</reference>; 2Ki 1:2.; <reference osisRef="1Chr.10.14">1Ch 10:14</reference>), and so here of superstitious trust in the physicians. Consequently it is not the mere inquiring of the physicians which is here censured, but only the godless manner in which Asa trusted in the physicians.
entries.2fdbbbcce12c3dec75f8894dacaf78e66060010b: <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.14">2Ch 16:14</reference> <div eID="gen6031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6032" type="x-p"/> The Chronicle gives a more exact account of Asa’s burial than 1Ki 15:24. He was buried in the city of David; not in the general tomb of the kings, however, but in a tomb which he had caused to be prepared for himself in that place. And they laid him upon the bed, which had been filled with spices (בּשׂמים, see <reference osisRef="Exod.30.23">Exo 30:23</reference>), and those of various kinds, mixed for an anointing mixture, prepared. זנים from זן, kind, species; וּזנים, <hi type="italic">et varia quidem</hi>. מרקּח in Piel only here, properly spiced, from רקח, to spice, usually to compound an unguent of various spices. מרקחת, the compounding of ointment; so also <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.30">1Ch 9:30</reference>, where it is usually translated by unguent. מעשׂה, work, manufacture, is a shortened <hi type="italic">terminus technicus</hi> for רוקח מעשׂה, manufacture of the ointment-compounder (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.30.25">Exo 30:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.35">Exo 30:35</reference>), and the conjecture that רוקח has been dropped out of the text by mistake is unnecessary. “And they kindled for him a great, very great burning,” cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.21.19">2Ch 21:19</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.34.5">Jer 34:5</reference>, whence we gather that the kindling of a burning, i.e., the burning of odorous spices, was customary at the burials of kings. Here it is only remarked that at Asa’s funeral an extraordinary quantity of spices was burnt. A burning of the corpse, or of the bed or clothes of the dead, is not to be thought of here: the Israelites were in the habit of burying their dead, not of burning them. That occurred only in extraordinary circumstances-as, for example, in the case of the bodies of Saul and his sons; see on 1Sa 31:12. The kindling and burning of spices at the solemn funerals of persons of princely rank, on the other hand, occurred also among other nations, e.g., among the Romans; cf. Plinii <hi type="italic">hist. nat.</hi> xii. 18, and M. Geier, <hi type="italic">de luctu Hebr.</hi> c. 6.  <chapter eID="2Chr.16"/> <div eID="gen6032" type="x-p"/>

entries.3946039b7e82a9ee8e8f95426cdd3063983b964b:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="16" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XVI.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 IN the six and thirtieth year of the reign of Asa <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>of the Kingdom of Asa, i. e.</ns0:hi> of the Kingdom of Judah, which was now Asa's Kingdom; or from the time of the division of the two Kingdoms. Rehoboam reigned 17 years, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 12. 13. Abijah 3 years, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 13. 2. Asa had now reigned 15 years, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 15. 10. all which put together make up the 35 years mentioned <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 15. 19. And in the next year Baasha wars against him; and the ground of War was the defection of many of his Subjects to Asa, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 15. 9. whom Asa endeavours to engage together with his own Subjects by an Oath and a Covenant to be true and faithful to God and con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sequently to himself, which was done in his 15th. year, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 15. 9, 10. and therefore in his 16th. year, called here the 36th. year of h<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>s Kingdom he commenceth an open War against him. If it be ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jected that <ns0:hi>the Reign,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Kingdom of Asa</ns0:hi> is otherwise understood of the time of Asa's personal Reign (as I may call it) <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 15. 10. The Answer is obvious, that there are many Instances in Scripture<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> (some of which have been formerly given, and others will be given in their proper places,) where the same Word or<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Phrase is taken differently, and that in the very same Chapter and History. And particularly this variety is elsewhere used both by Sacred and Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fane Writers, in the Computation of the years of Princes, which are sometimes reckoned from the beginning of their Reign, and sometimes from other remarkable Times and Occurrences. Thus Nebuchadnezzars years are sometimes computed from the begin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ning of his Reign, as 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 25. 8. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 52. 12, 29, 30. and some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />times from his compleat Conquest of Syria and Egypt, &c. As that Passage, <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 2. 1. <ns0:hi>In the second year of Nebuchadnezzar,</ns0:hi> is by the general stream of Interpreters understood. Thus Ahaziahs years, which doubtless were usually computed from the time of his Birth, are computed from another Head, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 22. 2. where see the Notes. And the like differences are observed in computing the years of some of the Syrian Monarchs and Roman Emperours, and particularly of Augustus, the years of whose Reign are variously ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />counted by the Roman Historians, sometimes from his first Consul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ship; sometimes from the time of the Triumvirate; and some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />times from that Famous Victory at Actium, where he utterly over<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />threw his Competitour, and made himself sole and unquestionable Emperour. And therefore it is not strange if it be so here.
